articles.title: Syke Community Base seeks activity providers for its Over 50s group in 2027
articles.excerpt: Syke Community Base is looking for activity providers, entertainers, tutors and speakers to run sessions for its Over 50s group throughout 2027.
articles.content_html:
Syke Community Base is looking for activity providers, entertainers, tutors and speakers to bring new sessions to its Over 50s group throughout 2027.

The community base is inviting people and organisations with activities that could appeal to the group to get in touch and discuss what they offer and their fees.

It is interested in a wide range of sessions, including talks and speakers, crafts and creative activities, singing and entertainment, classes and wellbeing activities, games and other activities suitable for the group.

The Over 50s group meets every Tuesday at 1pm.

Activity providers who are interested are asked to email Rebecca at Rebecca.SykeCB@outlook.com with a brief description of what they offer and their costs or fees.

Syke Community Base is also asking people to share the opportunity with providers who may be interested in delivering a session during 2027.
articles.legal_disclaimer: This article was compiled from information supplied by Syke Community Base. Details of activities, fees and availability should be confirmed directly with the organiser.

articles.title: Syke granted Conservation Area status to protect its historic character
articles.excerpt: Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, following a consultation in which 33 of 38 responses supported the designation.
articles.content_html:
Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, with the designation intended to protect the area's architectural and historic character from unsympathetic development.

The council confirmed the designation on 17 February 2026, describing Syke as an area with a unique and rich history. It highlighted the area's position on a historic packhorse route and its traditional weavers' cottages, including buildings with distinctive upper-floor windows designed to maximise natural light before electricity became widespread.

The Syke Conservation Area Appraisal provides further historical detail. It identifies Syke Road as part of the historic packhorse route linking Clitheroe with Rochdale and beyond, and records a network of historic paths across the Common, including remnants of the old packhorse trail.

The designated area covers Syke Common, parts of Dewhirst Road and Syke Road, and sections of Buckley Wood. The appraisal also identifies the northern extent of Cronkeyshaw Common and Syke Pond, well-preserved weavers' cottages, evidence of former industry, vernacular buildings and farmsteads, sandstone buildings, dry-stone and flagstone walls, and historic views and paths.

The appraisal includes historic maps from 1851, 1891, 1911 and 1936, alongside sections covering architectural character, historic buildings, key views and vistas, green spaces and the area's overall character. It provides the documented basis for the council's assessment of Syke's special architectural and historic interest.

### Public support for the designation

Rochdale Borough Council said more than 85% of locals backed the proposals. The consultation records 38 responses, of which 33 were positive about Conservation Area status for Syke. That represents approximately 87% of respondents, although the total number of responses was relatively small.

The responses nevertheless provide evidence of strong support among those who took part, as well as an indication that local heritage was an important consideration for respondents.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration, described the designation as a worthy addition to Rochdale's existing Conservation Areas and highlighted local engagement and pride in Syke's heritage.

### What Conservation Area status means

Conservation Areas are designated by local authorities where an area has special architectural or historic interest. Historic England guidance also provides for local authorities to prepare Conservation Area Appraisals setting out an area's character and significance.

The Syke appraisal states that its purpose is to explain the area's significance and identify measures to preserve and enhance its special character. It is intended to guide future development and inform future management plans. The document was prepared following consultation with local residents and draws on site visits, archive material, information from residents and Historic England guidance.

Historic England told Rochdale Daily that it had no involvement in the designation of the new Syke Conservation Area and directed us to its general guidance on Conservation Areas. Council documents show that Historic England guidance and documentation were considered during the process, but the designation itself was determined locally.

### Planning protections and what is not yet established

Conservation Area status introduces additional considerations within the planning process and can make permitted development rights more restrictive. The appraisal identifies circumstances where planning permission may be required, including substantial demolition of buildings or structures and certain works involving walls, gates, fences, extensions and alterations.

Article 4 Directions can remove further permitted development rights, but they are not automatic consequences of Conservation Area designation. The available information does not establish that an Article 4 Direction has been introduced for Syke.

The practical effect on individual properties will therefore depend on the planning controls that apply and any further decisions made by Rochdale Borough Council. The designation provides a framework for protecting Syke's special character, while the appraisal sets out the evidence and management considerations underpinning it.

articles.title: Prehistoric survivor growing in Syke herb garden has roots stretching back 300 million years
articles.excerpt: Residents picking herbs from a community garden in Syke are being invited to help tackle horsetail — a persistent weed whose ancestors grew locally more than 300 million years ago.
articles.content_html:
A troublesome weed growing in a community herb garden in Syke has a remarkable connection to the landscape's prehistoric past — with its ancestors dating back more than 300 million years.

Residents are being encouraged to help maintain the community herb garden while collecting fresh herbs to take home.

The garden is open for people to pick herbs for their own use, but volunteers are asking visitors who have a few spare minutes to lend a hand with some weeding at the same time.

One plant in particular is proving difficult to control: horsetail, also commonly known as mare's tail.

While modern gardeners may regard it as a persistent nuisance, horsetail belongs to an extraordinarily ancient group of plants whose history stretches back to long before dinosaurs walked the Earth.

During the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago, relatives of today's horsetails grew across the landscapes that would eventually become northern England.

Among them were Calamites — tree-like plants related to modern horsetails which could grow many metres tall and formed part of the vast Carboniferous vegetation.

Evidence of that lost landscape can still be found locally. A fossil discovered in a quarry at Tonacliffe shows the distinctive remains of Calamites, providing a physical connection between the plants growing here hundreds of millions of years ago and the much smaller horsetails residents battle in gardens today.

Carboniferous plant fossils can also be found within rocks across the surrounding moorland, reflecting a period when the area's environment looked dramatically different from the Pennine landscape residents know today.

People remain welcome to collect herbs from the community garden, but anyone visiting is being encouraged to pull a few weeds while they are there.

As the volunteers joked, nobody wants today's horsetail growing to the size of its Carboniferous grandparents.

The community garden is maintained for local people to enjoy, and even a few minutes of weeding can help keep it productive and accessible for everyone.

articles.title: Young bowlers invited to take part in Syke Bowling Club fun day
articles.excerpt: Syke Bowling Club is inviting young people from across Greater Manchester to a free Junior Fun Day featuring crown green bowling, prizes, refreshments and activities aimed at introducing more children to the sport.
articles.content_html:
Young people from across Greater Manchester are being invited to try crown green bowling at a free junior fun day taking place at Syke Bowling Club this weekend. The event is designed to introduce children and teenagers to the sport in a relaxed and welcoming environment, with food, drinks, prizes and coaching all included.

The Junior Fun Day will take place on Sunday, 2 August, at Syke Bowling Club on Dewhirst Road, Rochdale, with activities beginning at 11am. Organisers say the event is open to all juniors aged 18 and under, whether they have played crown green bowling before or are trying it for the first time.

Throughout the day, young participants will have the opportunity to take part in friendly bowling activities, meet other players and develop new skills under the guidance of club members. Organisers hope the event will encourage more young people to become involved in a sport that has a long history across Rochdale and the wider North West.

Prizes will be awarded during the event, including cash prizes, sweets and chocolate, while every junior attending will receive complimentary food, drinks and snacks. The organisers say the emphasis is on having fun, making new friends and giving children the confidence to have a go in an informal setting.

The event is also being used to appeal for local businesses and organisations to support junior bowling. Syke Bowling Club is seeking sponsors to help fund prizes and refreshments, saying contributions of any size would be welcomed to help expand opportunities for young players and support future events.

Grassroots sports clubs play an important role in communities by providing affordable activities, encouraging exercise and helping young people build confidence and friendships. Crown green bowling, while often associated with older generations, has seen clubs across the region working to attract younger players in an effort to secure the sport's long-term future.

Anyone interested in attending or finding out more can contact Lisa on 07900 493969. Organisers are encouraging families to come along, support the event and discover a sport that can be enjoyed by people of all ages.

With free refreshments, prizes and a welcoming atmosphere on offer, Syke Bowling Club hopes the Junior Fun Day will inspire the next generation of bowlers while showcasing one of Rochdale's long-established community sports clubs.
